title: Even the body stays
hook: the body you check in the mirror every day stays behind too; a hadith next door says what walks on
tomorrow: five lines the Buddha said to recite often. what are they?

segments.voice: Yesterday, wealth doesn't help: the house is burning, and what's given is carried out. It stays behind. Today, the last thing on the list, the closest one.

Mirrors, gym selfies, skincare steps, the hair that won't sit right: the body gets checked all day long. It's the one possession that feels like me. So if even the body stays behind, what goes on? The Buddha answers with a plain picture. And a neighbor tradition, Islam, answers with a funeral walk.
screen: `CHECKED ALL DAY LONG.` → `IT FEELS LIKE ME.` → `IF IT STAYS, WHAT GOES ON?`

segments.voice: The Dhammapada's picture is blunt. Before long, this body will lie on the ground, cast aside, without awareness, like a useless log. It isn't said to shame the body. It's the last of the third root's three steps: wealth stays, the people we love can't come along, and even the body stays. What goes on, in the Buddha's teaching, is kamma: the intentions a person acted on, and what they shaped. Now the neighbor. Muslims hand down a hadith, a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari. Three things follow the dead to the grave: family, wealth and deeds. Two go back home, and one stays with the person: their deeds. Hear how close that is. Family turns back at the graveside. The wealth goes home with the heirs. What walks on is what the person did. A Buddhist could nod at every word of that walk. And one honest difference. In Islam, Muslims believe deeds are brought before God, who judges with mercy, and that God will raise the dead on the Day of Resurrection. The Buddha's teaching has no judge: deeds bear their own fruit, the way seeds do, and the body left on the ground isn't raised again. Two neighbors, standing at the same graveside, agreeing on what walks on, and seeing different roads ahead.
screen: `LIKE A USELESS LOG.` · `WHAT GOES ON: KAMMA.` · `THREE FOLLOW; TWO GO BACK.` · `THE SAME GRAVESIDE, DIFFERENT ROADS.` · then, large: `EVEN THE BODY.`

segments.voice: Rest one hand on your chest and one on your belly, and feel the body breathing under them, a borrowed thing doing its work for now. With each out-breath, let a quiet thank you go to it. One day it stays behind; today, it's carrying you.
Even the body stays: at death the body is left behind too. What goes on is what a person did.
A line to keep: even the body, so thank it while it carries you. Day sixteen thirty-seven, held.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers pair Dhammapada 41 with gentle body practices so the reflection leads to gratitude, not disgust; at Muslim funerals, family and community walk the body to the grave, and the hadith of the three that follow is sometimes recalled.

match.prompt: what stays, what walks on — tap the pairs.
pairs: a body like a useless log

myth: Buddhism and Islam see what happens after death in exactly the same way
both say deeds walk on; Muslims believe God judges and raises the dead, and the Buddha's teaching has no judge.
a hadith says that of the three that follow the dead, only deeds remain with them
Sahih al-Bukhari: family and wealth go back; deeds stay with the person.
the 'useless log' verse is meant to make people hate their bodies
it's the last step of the third root: even the body stays. the practice that follows is gratitude.

fork.setup: at a friend's grandfather's janazah, a Muslim funeral, she tells you the hadith of the three that follow. she asks if Buddhists see it the same way. what's fair?
options: close on what walks on: deeds. different on what's ahead: God's judgment, or kamma with no judge.
exactly the same; every religion teaches this about death.
not at all; Buddhists don't think deeds matter after death.
fork.reveal: shared: family and wealth turn back, deeds walk on. different: Muslims believe God judges and raises the dead; the Buddha taught deeds bear their own fruit.

chat.meaning: Even the body stays behind. In the Buddha's teaching what goes on is kamma, what a person did, and a hadith says deeds walk on too.

tie.story: The Dhammapada says the body will lie on the ground; a hadith says family and wealth turn back and deeds go on.

tie.you: what would you want to walk on after you?

Dhammapada's.meaning: of the Dhammapada, a collection of the Buddha's sayings in verse

kamma.meaning: intentional action and what it shapes (Sanskrit karma)

hadith.meaning: a report of the Prophet Muhammad's words or deeds

Sahih al-Bukhari.meaning: a major collection of hadith, gathered by Imam al-Bukhari

sources.ref: Dhammapada 41 (before long this body will lie on the earth, cast aside, without consciousness, like a useless log)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6514 (three follow the dead: family, wealth and deeds; two return and one remains, the deeds)
the third root's three points (wealth, loved ones and the body cannot help at death), as taught in the Tibetan lamrim

notes: Wisdom shape with the unity thread: shared (family and wealth turn back; deeds walk on) and one honest difference (Muslims believe God judges with mercy and raises the dead on the Day of Resurrection; the Buddha's teaching has no judge, deeds bear their own fruit). Never 'all the same'; the myth, fork and chat test exactly that. Please have the Islam Keeper check the hadith and the description of Muslim belief.
Sahih al-Bukhari 6514 paraphrased (also in Sahih Muslim 2960); confirm numbering. The honorific 'peace be upon him' is used at the Prophet's first mention.
Dhammapada 41 paraphrased (Max Müller's wording not verified, so not quoted).
'Kamma... the body left on the ground isn't raised again': a fair summary of Buddhist teaching (rebirth is not bodily resurrection); confirm wording with the Buddhist Keeper.
The fork mentions a janazah (Muslim funeral) for a friend's grandfather as a hypothetical; no claim about how all Muslim funerals run. howItsDone says the hadith is 'sometimes recalled'.
Organ donation was deliberately avoided as a storyline (Buddhist views differ).
